summary:
FlameSafe is a web app built on NASA’s Physical Science Informatics archive: all 24 microgravity combustion investigations and all 1,995 of their test rows. Pick a material, an oxygen level and a pressure, or type the question in plain English, and it answers from the real test data with a grade for the evidence behind that answer. Measured means a test exists at those conditions. Bounded means tests exist above and below. No data means nobody has run it, and the app then shows the closest test that does exist and why it may not transfer.

The challenge asks what microgravity combustion data tells us about fire safety beyond low Earth orbit. Our answer includes what it cannot tell us. No solid material has ever been tested above 22.2% oxygen, and the planned lunar habitat runs at 30% or more. Of 1,995 tests, 476 reach that oxygen level, but only 66 also meet the 10.2 psi ceiling, and all 66 are gas burner flames rather than burning solids. 87 of 132 material-and-oxygen combinations hold no test at all.

This matters because habitat material selection is being decided now, flammability rises sharply with oxygen, and a tool that answered every question confidently would bury the gap. A language model only reads the question and words the reply; every number is computed from the source tables and checked against them, and 18 self-tests fail the build if any claim stops being true
details:
What it does. FlameSafe answers one question honestly: if you put a material in a spacecraft atmosphere, does NASA actually know whether it will burn? You pick a material, an oxygen level and a pressure. Before any number appears, the answer carries a grade. Measured means a test exists at those conditions. Bounded means tests exist above and below, so the answer is interpolated rather than observed. No data means nobody has run it, and the screen then shows the nearest real test and why it may not transfer.

How it works. A four-step pipeline pulls all 24 Combustion Science investigations and their 22 experimental data tables from NASA’s Physical Science Informatics API, reconciles them into one schema of 1,995 test rows, and grades every query against those rows. A language model is used at two points only: it reads an English question into a structured query, and it words the final reply from a list of facts the deterministic code has already computed. Any number it returns must appear in the question, and any number in its prose must appear in those facts. Either failure discards the model’s output and falls back to fixed rules. The model is structurally unable to supply a figure.

What we found. No solid material has ever been tested above 22.2% oxygen — PMMA and Nomex stop there, SIBAL cloth at 20.8%, Japan wax at 17.4%. A lunar habitat is planned at 30% oxygen or more and 10.2 psi or less. Of 1,995 tests, 476 clear that oxygen floor, but only 66 also clear the pressure ceiling, and all 66 are gas burner flames. No solid and no liquid droplet has been tested in both habitat conditions at once. The gap map shows it directly: 87 of 132 material-by-oxygen cells hold no test, 69 of them above the habitat floor.

Benefit and intended impact. A materials engineer gets a defensible answer, or an honest absence, in seconds instead of a literature search. The 87 empty cells are not a limitation of the tool but a research agenda: a concrete list of experiments worth flying, derived from what the archive does not contain. Flammability rises sharply with oxygen, so extrapolating from 22.2% to 30% is exactly the kind of confident guess that gets people hurt.

What makes it creative. Most tools built on a dataset are search tools, and most tools built with a language model answer every question asked. FlameSafe does the opposite of both. It refuses. It also refuses to pool incomparable evidence: a droplet extinction diameter and a flame-spread rate measure different physical quantities, so the tool declines to chart them on one axis and prints the physical reason instead. The language model earns its place by being kept away from the numbers.

What we had to consider. NASA’s tables disagree on units — one file records oxygen as 21, another as 0.21 — so each column is checked against the range of its own values before conversion, not trusted by its name. Outcome codes differ per table and are decoded explicitly rather than by keyword. 187 free-text fuel strings collapse to 25 materials; an unrecognised one stays null rather than being guessed. 14 materials were tested with no oxygen level recorded at all, which is a different kind of gap and is shown as one. 18 self-tests assert every figure above and fail the build if the data stops supporting them.

Built with. TypeScript throughout; Node for the data pipeline; React, Vite and Tailwind for the dashboard, with no charting library — the visuals are plain SVG and CSS. Claude Sonnet sits behind both number guards. Deployed on Vercel with the question endpoint as a serverless function. The repository rebuilds the dataset byte-for-byte from committed CC0 inputs with no API key, so anyone can verify every number.

NASA data used. Physical Science Informatics (psi.nasa.gov), CC0-1.0. All 24 Combustion Science investigations and their 22 data tables — 1,995 test rows, 1,139 with a recorded oxygen level. FLEX and FLEX-2 droplet burns, BASS and BASS-II solid flame spread, the ACME burner series, CFI cool flames, DAFT smoke detection. 1,976 rows were run on the ISS in the Combustion Integrated Rack and the Microgravity Science Glovebox, 11 flew on Cygnus, and 8 come from a principal investigator’s ground laboratory. Every investigation keeps its DOI and every row links back to its source file.
